content: Physical exercise training has the potential to enhance muscle function and cardiorespiratory capacity in individuals with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). By optimizing aerobic capacity and utilizing the remaining muscle tissue, exercise may help mitigate the progressive muscle deterioration caused by motor neuron loss and inactivity in SMA. However, there is currently no comprehensive synthesis of evidence regarding the effects of physical exercise training in individuals with SMA type 3. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of physical exercise training on functional performance in individuals with SMA type 3 and to identify any associated adverse effects. A systematic search was conducted on May 8, 2018, across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Specialised Register, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, AMED, and LILACS. Additional searches for ongoing trials were performed on April 25, 2018, in NHSEED, DARE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). The inclusion criteria for the review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs lasting at least 12 weeks, comparing physical exercise training (strength training, aerobic exercise, or a combination of both) to placebo, standard care, or non-physical interventions in individuals with SMA type 3. Participants included both adults and children aged five years or older, with a confirmed genetic diagnosis of SMA type 3 (Kugelberg-Welander syndrome). Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were employed for data collection and analysis. The review included one RCT that investigated the effects of a six-month, home-based program combining muscle strength training and recumbent cycle ergometry compared to usual care in 14 ambulatory individuals with SMA type 3. Participants ranged in age from 10 to 48 years. The study was evaluator-blinded, but neither participants nor personnel could be blinded to the intervention, introducing a high risk of bias. While participants adhered to the prescribed strength training, only 50% achieved the intended aerobic exercise regimen. The primary outcome measure was the change in walking distance on the six-minute walk test (6MWT). A minimal detectable change in this test is 24.0 meters. After six months, the training group showed an average increase of 9.4 meters, while the usual care group showed a decrease of 0.14 meters. The mean difference between groups was 9.54 meters (95% confidence interval [CI]: -83.04 to 102.12; N = 12), which was not statistically significant. Cardiopulmonary exercise capacity was assessed by changes in peak oxygen uptake (VO2max). The training group experienced a decrease of 0.12 mL/kg/min, while the usual care group showed a decrease of 1.34 mL/kg/min. The mean difference between groups was 1.22 mL/kg/min (95% CI: -2.16 to 4.6; N = 12). A clinically meaningful increase in VO2max is considered to be 3.5 mL/kg/min, which was not achieved in this study. Functional performance was also evaluated using the Hammersmith Functional Motor Scale Expanded (HFMSE), which has a scoring range of 0 to 66. An increase of 3 or more points is considered clinically meaningful. The training group demonstrated a 2-point increase in HFMSE scores over six months, while the usual care group showed no change. The mean difference between groups was 2.00 points (95% CI: -2.06 to 6.06; N = 12), which was not statistically significant. Muscle strength was measured using the Manual Muscle Testing (MMT) total score, which ranges from 28 (weakest) to 280 (strongest). The training group showed an increase of 6.8 points in the MMT total score, compared to a decrease of 5.14 points in the usual care group. The mean difference between groups was 11.94 points (95% CI: -3.44 to 27.32; N = 12), indicating a slight improvement in muscle strength in the training group. The study reported no statistically significant effects of the training program on fatigue or quality of life. The certainty of evidence for all outcomes was rated as very low due to methodological limitations and imprecision. The study did not evaluate the effects of physical exercise training on overall physical activity levels. No serious adverse events or adverse events leading to withdrawal were reported, but the very low certainty of evidence limits the ability to draw broader conclusions. In conclusion, it remains uncertain whether combined strength and aerobic exercise training is beneficial or harmful for individuals with SMA type 3 due to the very low quality of evidence. Further well-designed and adequately powered studies, adhering to international standards for exercise intervention development, are needed to better understand the response to exercise in this population and to establish evidence-based exercise guidelines for SMA type 3.
